analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced beyond its committee referral and never received a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal prohibition on oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain and order the Interior Department to set up a leasing program there, with the first sale of at least 200,000 acres within 18 months. It would narrow environmental review by barring the department from studying a no-leasing alternative, declare drilling compatible with the refuge's purposes without further findings, and cap development footprint at 2,000 surface acres. Royalties would be at least 12.5%, with lease terms covering reclamation, seasonal drilling closures for caribou calving, and Alaska Native hiring preferences, plus a small impact-aid fund for affected local communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that would win drilling leases on the coastal plain, the Alaska Native corporations receiving conveyed land title, and Alaska communities slated for impact-aid money.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the statutory ban on producing oil and gas from the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, the first legal step to opening the coastal plain to leasing.
Directs the Interior Department to run a competitive leasing program, hold a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres within 18 months, and a second sale a year later.

Declares drilling compatible with the refuge's purposes without further findings and directs the department not to study a no-leasing alternative, reducing legal and procedural obstacles for developers.
Caps the total surface footprint of development at 2,000 acres and requires best available technology, reclamation bonds, and seasonal drilling limits around caribou calving areas.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the loss of a wilderness area preserved for four decades and the risk of habitat and subsistence damage; federal taxpayers forgo land that would otherwise remain unleased.

drawbacks.text: The bill forbids the Interior Department from analyzing a no-leasing alternative and deems the 1987 environmental impact statement sufficient for preleasing decisions made decades later, limiting up-to-date environmental review.
Drilling in the coastal plain would affect habitat for caribou, polar bears, and migratory birds and subsistence uses valued by Alaska Native communities in the region.
Opening the refuge to leasing has been contentious for decades, and the bill's advance of drilling without a full no-action analysis was widely criticized by opponents as foreclosing public review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect is transferring a protected federal wilderness area to energy development, with a revenue stream and modest local impact aid in return. Weighing the loss of a unique refuge against uncertain oil output and a capped fund is the core tradeoff Congress chose not to resolve.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so no floor vote ever occurred.

narrative.text: Murkowski introduced the bill on February 12, 2015, and it was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
No further committee action, hearing markup, or floor vote is recorded in the action history.
Only one Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and no Democratic support is recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of coastal plain drilling, including environmental and Alaska Native interests who wanted the refuge left intact, benefit from the bill stalling; oil and gas companies gain nothing since no leases were authorized by this bill.

for.name: Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and chaired the committee to which it was referred, though no markup was scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote or committee action ever took place, so no recorded opposition exists in the congressional record; the bill had one Republican cosponsor and no Democratic support.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is opening a currently off-limits federal area to leasing, directly benefiting energy companies. Public benefits cited include royalties and local impact aid, though opponents note environmental and subsistence costs.
